sources.citation: Linnasalo, Katri. 2003. Nek Phonology Essentials. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG. 81 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives / REAP; PDF title 'phone essentials unicode').
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: NEK (not Nuk): word stress falls on the first syllable whose nucleus is not schwa; if every nucleus is schwa, on the first syllable; four-syllable words have secondary stress on the third syllable; stressed open syllables are lengthened (no underlying length contrast); verbs have their own pattern with secondary stresses from certain affixes (sec. 4.1.3); appendix wordlists note 'Stress is on the first syllable unless indicated otherwise.' Intonation (4.2) is a descending pitch contour; no tone.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1984. A linguistic field guide to the Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. PL D-57. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: '(70) Nuk (pop. 1,720)' with North/South dialect village lists; no phonology, silent on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1975. North-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene, 527-567. Pacific Linguistics C-38. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: Nuk entry is demographic: village list and 'There are two dialects, Northern and Southern, determined on the basis of lexicostatistics'; notes Nek speakers of Guombot and Wampangan 'are largely bilingual with NUK'. Family-wide phonology (phoneme Table A, syllable structure, morphophonemics) is given for representative languages only (Erap = Urii); the words stress/accent/tone/pitch do not occur anywhere in the chapter.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11, 45-78. Pacific Linguistics A-23. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 2.7.11 on Nuk is demographic only ('spoken by 1800 people living east of Boana. There is little dialectal variation'). Sec. 6.1 phonology represents the Erap family by Uri with no stress statement; the only stress remark is 'Stress is phonemic in Rawa but probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat' (and contrastive on few words in Suroi). Nothing on Nuk stress.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. & K. A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District - New Guinea. In Wurm & Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell, 1065-1094. PL C-13.
sources.note: Checklist entry '23. Nuk (1,800)' only; silent on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1970. The Trans-New Guinea Phylum: explorations in deep-level genetic relationships. Pacific Linguistics B-16. Canberra: Australian National University. v+107 pp. hdl:1885/146444.
sources.note: No phonology content for Nuk: Nuk forms are cited in a handful of cognate sets (e.g. 'ERA j dAm', 'ERA j matuk', 'ERA j mane', 'ERA j endzi') in phonetic transcription without stress or pitch marks; the whole monograph contains zero occurrences of stress/accent/tonal/pitch/prosod- (whitespace-collapsed search; the 6 'tone' hits are 'stone'/'but one'). Wordlist-level data only, no statement.
